implementation_notes: The canonical C++ realization: the body embeds its count (a std::atomic<unsigned> once handles can cross threads) and two free functions next to the type - intrusive_ptr_add_ref and intrusive_ptr_release - implement the protocol; boost::intrusive_ptr<T> calls them unqualified through argument-dependent lookup on construction, copy and destruction, and the release function destroys the body when the count reaches zero. What replaces the classic hand-written handle: the smart-pointer template itself - no copy constructor, assignment operator or destructor is written, and the handle stays the size of a raw pointer because the count lives in the object. The Boost documentation recommends trying a shared_ptr-based design first; choose intrusive_ptr when the count must be in the object (fixed layout, foreign objects, no extra allocation) or when handles must be constructible from raw pointers.
pitfalls: The counter is initialised to 0 here because intrusive_ptr increments on construction; initialise the field and every path that hands out a body consistently, or the first release frees an object still in use.
intrusive_ptr_release must not throw and must destroy exactly once; releasing a pointer that did not come from an intrusive handle, or releasing it twice, is undefined behaviour.
Mixing intrusive_ptr and shared_ptr on the same object gives it two counts and a double delete; keep one ownership model per body.

variants.name: boost::intrusive_ref_counter CRTP base (policy-selected counter)
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of writing the hooks by hand, the body derives from boost::intrusive_ref_counter<Derived, CounterPolicy>, which provides both the count and the intrusive_ptr_add_ref/intrusive_ptr_release overloads; the policy selects the cost - thread_safe_counter (the default) for objects whose handles can cross threads, thread_unsafe_counter for thread-confined ones. The CRTP parameter is what lets the base destroy the correct most-derived object at zero. Choose this when you own the class, want the least code, and accept inheritance (and an empty base) as the price.
pitfalls: Destruction goes through the CRTP-typed base, so passing the wrong Derived type destroys the wrong object at zero.
thread_unsafe_counter omits the atomic operations entirely - correct only while every handle stays on one thread, so pick the policy deliberately.
The count is not directly controllable (use_count only), and branching on it reintroduces the concurrency bug the policy was meant to prevent.

variants.name: Adopt a foreign counted object (COM, Core Foundation, GObject)
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's original motivation in Boost: OS and framework objects already carry their own count (COM IUnknown has AddRef/Release; Core Foundation uses CFRetain/CFRelease; GObject uses g_object_ref/unref), and only the handle is missing. Define the two ADL functions as one-line forwarders to the foreign protocol and adopt a reference the caller already holds with intrusive_ptr(p, false) - the constructor increments only when add_ref is true - or let it increment by default when taking a new reference from a valid pointer. No count is added to the object; the handle simply speaks the foreign protocol.
pitfalls: intrusive_ptr(p, false) consumes a reference: the caller must transfer ownership rather than reuse p, or the object is released while still in use.
The forwarding hooks must be found by ADL in the object's namespace (or fall back to namespace boost); a hook for the wrong type counts the wrong object.
Foreign protocols differ (COM Release returns a count, CF/GObject do not); never combine a foreign count with a C++-owned count on the same object.
